title: Compromise Host Software Binary
summary: This technique is persistence by replacing or patching software that the host already runs. An adversary targets an executable that users, services or scheduled jobs invoke routinely, such as an SSH client, a file transfer tool, a mail client or a browser, and either swaps it for a backdoored copy or patches the existing file so that malicious code runs before normal execution resumes. Patching techniques include altering the entry point or hooking imported functions so the original behaviour is preserved and the user notices nothing, and an SSH client modified this way quietly records credentials at every login. The same code can also be delivered as a trojanised update, and attackers often pin the package version so the modified binary is not replaced by the next update. Detection relies on file integrity monitoring of application paths, mismatched package checksums or signatures, unexpected listening processes, and version pinning in package manager configuration.

beginner.definition: Programs you already trust can be changed so they also run hidden attacker code. This technique is when an attacker edits or replaces software on a computer, such as a remote login tool. The program still works normally, so nobody suspects it, and the attacker keeps access.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modified software is hard to notice because the program still does its job. The change survives restarts and often survives updates. It can also collect passwords each time you log in. This gives the attacker a quiet, long-lasting way back into the machine.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a program that people or services run every single day.
They replace that program file with a copy that hides extra attacker code.
The copy runs its hidden code first, then passes control to the normal program.
The user sees the usual behaviour and does not suspect that anything changed.
The attacker also blocks updates so the modified program is not overwritten.
They return later through the same trusted program and keep their access.
beginner.example: Think of a shop that uses a trusted cash register to log every sale. A thief opens the register, adds a small extra part, and closes it again. The register still prints receipts and still counts money, so the shopkeeper notices nothing. The added part quietly copies every card number that passes through, just as a patched login tool copies every password.
takeaways: Watch the integrity of the programs you already trust, not only new files.
Unexpected version pinning in a package manager can protect a modified binary.
Compare installed files against vendor checksums or signatures on a schedule.

objectives: Explain what compromising a host software binary means and why it provides persistence.
Describe how patching an entry point preserves normal program behaviour.
Identify which file and process telemetry can reveal a modified binary.
Recognise version pinning as a way of preventing updates from removing the change.
Recommend integrity monitoring and update controls for application paths.
